Nevertheless, these attributes alone do not guarantee the commercial success of PSCs, as any emerging technology must also demonstrate operational stabilities already achieved by other mature PV systems with degradation rates of 0.5% to 1% per year over a lifespan of 20 to 25 years.34,35 To date, the operational lifetimes of PSCs are limited to several months at best, constituting an important roadblock in their deployment.1,3,36–39 A significant factor limiting the operational lifetimes of PSCs is their rapid degradation upon exposure to atmospheric gasses such as oxygen and moisture, and robust protection strategies are essential for overcoming this limitation.1–6 While standard glass- to-glass encapsulation provides impermeable surfaces,40–42 ingress from adhesive joints and protruding metal grids is a concern. In such cases, thin-film encapsulations offer a secondary protection strategy that can prolong the operational lifetime of PSCs.7 Additionally, standalone thin-film encapsulations without glass covers play a vital role in advancing perovskite-based technologies, which aim to reduce weight, enhance flexibility, improve heat transfer, and optimize light management.8–15 Moreover, thin-film encapsulations possess an innovative quality that deserves further exploration: electrical conductivity.16–20 In the following sections, we briefly cover existing thin-film encapsulation technologies to then focus on encapsulations composed of conductive materials, also known as transparent conductive gas diffusion barriers (TCGDB). To achieve high electrical conductivities and low permeation rates,43–45 TCGDBs typically require inorganic materials such as metals and metal oxides (e.g., transparent conductive oxide, ultra-thin- metal) with a defect-free microstructure.46–50 We observe the tendency of inorganic films to form and propagate diffusion pathways (e.g., pores and pinholes) as a significant 4/52 DE-EE0010241 Nicolas Gaillard technological hurdle and emphasize the importance of passivation strategies to reduce permeability.49,51–57 Most notably, it is observed that TCGDBs have yet to implement state-of-the-art polymer-based passivation techniques, particularly the inorganic/organic multilayer, due to the electrically insulating nature of polymers. To address the electrically insulating properties of polymers, we present the transparent conductive composite (TCC), which offers anisotropic electrical conductivity, enabling the development of an inorganic/polymer-composite TCGDB. This innovative encapsulating electrode represents a pioneering advancement, leveraging the advantages of integrating polymers alongside inorganic thin films (i.e., an inorganic/polymer multilayer structure) to mitigate diffusion pathways and enhance the operational stability of PSCs.
